title: Eurozone Inflation Slows to 2.8% in June as Energy Eases
summary: Eurostat's flash estimate put euro area annual inflation at 2.8% in June 2026, down from 3.2% in May, with energy inflation easing to 8.7%, services at 3.2% and the rate excluding energy, food, alcohol and tobacco at 2.4%.
description:
Annual inflation in the euro area slowed to 2.8% in June 2026, according to the flash estimate published by Eurostat, the statistical office of the European Union, on July 1, 2026. That compares with 3.2% in May. On the month, consumer prices were down 0.1%. The release is the first look at the June data, and Eurostat marks every figure in it as an estimate. This article sets out the numbers in the release, what drove the slowdown, how the largest member countries compared, and what readers should and should not conclude from a flash estimate. It does not offer financial advice.

The headline numbers

Eurostat measures inflation with the Harmonised Index of Consumer Prices, known as HICP. The all-items rate of 2.8% in June followed 3.2% in May. The monthly change of minus 0.1% means that the average basket of goods and services was slightly cheaper in June than in May, which is a notable detail after a period of elevated energy costs.

The release breaks the figure into its main parts. Energy inflation was 8.7% in June, down from 10.8% in May, and energy prices fell 1.7% on the month. Food, alcohol and tobacco rose 1.6% over the year, down from 1.9%, and fell 0.2% on the month. Non-energy industrial goods were up 0.9% over the year, the same pace as in May, with a monthly fall of 0.2%. Services rose 3.2% over the year, down from 3.5%, and increased 0.4% on the month.

The measure often called core

The Eurostat release does not use the word core. The closest measure is the rate excluding energy, food, alcohol and tobacco, which was 2.4% in June, down from 2.6% in May, with a monthly rate of 0.2%. A second measure, all items excluding energy, stood at 2.2% in June, down from 2.4% in May. Analysts and news reports commonly describe the first of these as core inflation, and readers should be aware that different institutions define core slightly differently.

What drove the slowdown

The largest contribution came from energy. The year-on-year energy rate is still high at 8.7%, but it has come down by more than two percentage points in a month, and energy prices fell on a monthly basis. Food, alcohol and tobacco also slowed, and services eased by three tenths of a point. Non-energy industrial goods were unchanged in annual terms. Taken together, the details point to a broad but moderate cooling rather than a single cause. The release does not explain the reasons behind the energy move, and this article does not add a cause that the source does not state.

Services deserve a note. At 3.2%, the services rate remains above the headline figure, and it increased 0.4% on the month. Services prices tend to follow labour costs more than commodity prices, so they are usually watched closely by central banks. A reading that stays above 3% can mean that domestic price pressure is slower to fade than the energy-driven part of inflation.

How the member countries compared

Eurostat reports rates for each member state. Germany was at 2.4% in June, France at 2.0%, Italy at 3.1% and Spain at 3.6%. The highest rate among members was Lithuania at 5.5%, and the lowest was Malta at 1.9%. Other rates in the release included Belgium at 3.0%, Ireland at 3.2%, Greece at 3.9%, Austria at 3.1%, Portugal at 3.1%, Finland at 2.7% and Estonia at 2.0%. The spread between Malta and Lithuania, more than three and a half points, shows how uneven price growth remains across the currency area even when the average cools.

The Netherlands was an exception in the data. The release says it did not supply figures in time, and Eurostat estimated them only so that the euro area totals could be calculated. Eurostat also noted that Germany updated its 2026 item weights in June, which changed the euro area weights as well, and that services figures for February and March 2026 were revised. Since January 2026 the euro area has had 21 members following the inclusion of Bulgaria, and earlier data reflect the 20-member group, handled with a chain index.

Why a flash estimate is provisional

Eurostat issues the flash estimate at the end of each reference month, using early information from member states. The complete HICP release follows around the middle of the following month, and the schedule in this case showed the full June data due on July 17, 2026, with the next flash estimate on July 31. Flash figures can be revised, so a single reading should be treated as an early indication. The 0.4 point drop in the headline rate is a meaningful move, but a trend is better judged over several months.

What it means for households and borrowers

Slower inflation does not mean prices are falling. An annual rate of 2.8% means that the typical basket still costs 2.8% more than a year earlier, although the monthly decline in June shows that the pace has eased. For savers, a lower inflation rate reduces the erosion of purchasing power on cash balances. For people with variable-rate loans or mortgages across the euro area, the direction of inflation matters because it feeds into the decisions of the European Central Bank. One market preview ahead of the bank's July 23 meeting expected it to hold its deposit rate, with a possible increase in September, but that is a forecast from a commentator and not a decision, and readers should check the bank's own announcements.

What to watch next

Three data points are worth following. The first is the full June release for confirmation or revision of the flash numbers. The second is the services rate, to see whether it moves closer to the headline. The third is energy, since the annual rate of 8.7% is still high and will depend on price developments in the months ahead. Eurostat publishes all of these on its website. This article summarizes official statistics and is for general information only, not financial advice.
image_alt: Euro banknotes representing eurozone inflation trends (illustrative)
key_points: Eurostat's flash estimate put euro area annual inflation at 2.8% in June 2026, down from 3.2% in May, with prices down 0.1% on the month.
Energy inflation eased to 8.7% from 10.8%, services slowed to 3.2% from 3.5%, food, alcohol and tobacco slowed to 1.6%, and non-energy industrial goods held at 0.9%.
Inflation excluding energy, food, alcohol and tobacco was 2.4%, down from 2.6% in May, and excluding energy alone it was 2.2%, down from 2.4%.
Among the largest members, Germany was at 2.4%, France at 2.0%, Italy at 3.1% and Spain at 3.6%, with Lithuania highest at 5.5% and Malta lowest at 1.9%.
The figures are a flash estimate marked provisional, and Eurostat scheduled the full June data for July 17, 2026.
why_it_matters: Consumer prices in the euro area shape interest rate decisions, mortgage costs and the real value of wages and savings across 21 countries. A slower rate, driven mainly by energy, eases pressure on household budgets, but services inflation above 3% shows that price growth in the part of the economy tied to wages has not yet fully cooled.

title: APRA Finalises Capital Treatment of Longevity Products, Effective July 1, 2026: Insurers Can Use an 'Advanced Illiquidity Premium' With a 45% Floor and Extra Controls
summary: On March 31, 2026 APRA finalised amendments letting life insurers use an 'advanced illiquidity premium' to set capital for longevity products, with added governance, reporting and asset controls and a 45% floor kept after consultation; the changes took effect on July 1, 2026.
description:
Australia's prudential regulator has changed how life insurers must hold capital against products that pay income for life, in an effort to make such products easier to offer. The Australian Prudential Regulation Authority (APRA) released a response paper on March 31, 2026, finalising amendments to the capital treatment of longevity products, according to a summary by the law firm Regulation Tomorrow. The changes took effect on July 1, 2026. They followed consultations in June 2025 and October 2025, and APRA published an attachment summarising changes from the October 2025 versions.

Longevity products are insurance products that guarantee income for as long as the policyholder lives, such as lifetime annuities. They expose the insurer to longevity risk, the risk that people live longer than expected, and the insurer must hold capital against it. Because the insurer's promises stretch over decades and are usually matched with long-term, relatively illiquid assets, the way capital rules treat the link between those assets and liabilities has large effects on the cost of the product.

The core change is optional. Insurers can choose to use what APRA calls an "advanced illiquidity premium" (AILP) to set their capital requirements for these products. An illiquidity premium is the extra return available from assets that cannot easily be sold, and the AILP lets an insurer recognise more of it when it values long-term liabilities backed by such assets. APRA paired the option with added controls on governance, reporting and the assets backing the portfolio. The regulator's aim is to allow capital requirements to reflect the long-term nature of the liabilities while retaining safeguards for policyholders.

Consultation feedback, according to the summary, was broadly positive. Some respondents asked for changes to the risk allowance floor and to how the AILP applies in the credit spread stress charge under the life insurance prudential standard LPS 114. Views on the restrictions on assets were mixed. APRA decided to keep the AILP settings, saying they "remain sound and strike the right balance" between capital efficiency and risk controls. It made wording changes: eligible products are called "longevity products" in the response paper and "illiquid liabilities" in the standards.

The most debated point was the 45% floor. APRA kept it. The regulator acknowledged that the floor limits the capital benefit when credit spreads are very narrow, as they are now, and that in those conditions the AILP may be equal to the Standard Illiquidity Premium, meaning the new option would offer no extra benefit. However, its historical analysis found that such conditions are rare, so the evidence did not justify lowering the floor. In plain terms, insurers hoping for large capital savings today may find that the benefit is smaller than they would like while credit spreads are tight, though the option may be worth more if spreads widen.

For implementation, APRA released a reporting template for insurers using the AILP and sought feedback on it by May 12, 2026. The July 1 start date meant insurers could begin using the option from the start of the new financial year, though the sources reviewed do not say how many insurers plan to do so.

The policy sits within a wider effort to improve retirement incomes. Australia's superannuation system has accumulated large balances, and as more members move into retirement the question of how to turn savings into reliable income becomes more pressing. APRA's stated direction, as summarised, is to let insurers invest in sustainable, competitively priced products that help Australians retire with confidence, although the response paper summary reviewed here does not quote a named APRA member on the point.

What should readers make of it? The change is permissive, not mandatory, and it reduces a technical barrier to product design and does not itself create demand. Whether insurers launch more lifetime income products depends on pricing, investment opportunities, distribution through super funds and consumer interest. The 45% floor means the capital relief will not be as large as some insurers wanted, and the added asset controls mean that those who use the option must meet governance and reporting standards.

There are also questions about risk. A more generous recognition of illiquidity can reduce capital held against long-term liabilities, and APRA has chosen to pair it with restrictions to prevent insurers from taking on excessive risk in search of yield. How those restrictions work in practice, and how strictly they are supervised, will determine whether the framework strengthens or weakens policyholder protection. The summary notes that views on the asset restrictions were mixed, which suggests the details will continue to be debated.

For consumers, the immediate effect is none: policies already in force are unaffected, and any new products will take time to appear. For the industry, the next steps are to decide whether to adopt the AILP, to prepare the required governance and reporting, and to watch how APRA applies the floor. The regulator's analysis implies that the answer will depend heavily on the credit-spread environment, which is outside insurers' control.
source_name: Regulation Tomorrow (summary of APRA's March 31, 2026 response paper) and APRA
image_alt: Retirement savings paperwork representing longevity and lifetime income products (illustrative)
key_points: APRA issued a response paper on March 31, 2026 finalising amendments to the capital treatment of longevity products, effective July 1, 2026, after consultations in June and October 2025.

Insurers may choose to use an 'advanced illiquidity premium' (AILP) to set their capital requirements for these products, paired with added controls on governance, reporting and the assets backing the portfolio.
APRA kept the AILP settings, saying they 'remain sound and strike the right balance' between capital efficiency and risk controls, and retained a 45% floor.
APRA acknowledged that the floor limits the capital benefit when credit spreads are very narrow, but its historical analysis found such conditions are rare.
Eligible products are called 'longevity products' in the response paper and 'illiquid liabilities' in the standards, and APRA released a reporting template for insurers using the AILP.
why_it_matters: Australians are retiring with large superannuation balances and need ways to turn savings into lifetime income. Lower or more stable capital requirements could make it cheaper for insurers to offer guaranteed lifetime income products, while APRA's controls aim to keep those promises safe.

title: FCA's CP26/18 Proposes Six Mortgage Rule Changes, From Quarterly Payment Schedules for Variable Incomes to Narrowing the 'Credit-Impaired' Definition and Capping Bridging Loans at 24 Months, With Responses Due July 28
summary: The UK Financial Conduct Authority published consultation paper CP26/18 on June 9, 2026, proposing changes to six areas of its mortgage rules, including interest-only lending, retirement interest-only, variable income, foreign-currency loans, the credit-impaired definition and bridging loans, with responses due by July 28 and a policy statement intended for the second half of 2026.
description:
On June 9, 2026, the UK's Financial Conduct Authority published consultation paper CP26/18, titled "Mortgage Rule Review: Supporting first-time buyers and underserved consumers". The paper proposes changes to the regulator's mortgage rules in six areas. It is a consultation, which means the FCA is asking for views before deciding; none of the proposals is yet in force. This article is based on the FCA's press release of the same date and on law-firm summaries of the paper, and it does not reproduce the full rule text, which readers should consult in the consultation paper itself.

Where the paper sits in the review

CP26/18 is one step in a wider Mortgage Rule Review. According to a law-firm summary, it follows Discussion Paper DP25/2 of June 2025 and Feedback Statement FS25/6 of December 2025. The FCA says in its press release that it set out plans to reform the mortgage market in December 2025. The same summary says the FCA is continuing policy work on three other themes of the review: lending in later life, enabling innovation, and protecting consumers in vulnerable circumstances. Those themes are not part of CP26/18.

The FCA's stated aim and its evidence

The press release says the proposals would encourage lenders to assess affordability using a person's full and current situation, rather than excluding people over minor or past credit history issues. It adds that lenders would face fewer barriers to offering flexible repayments for people with variable income and to lending to people paid in foreign currency, and that the proposals include supporting consumers in understanding their options. David Geale, the FCA's executive director for payments and digital finance, said: "Our mortgage rules need to keep pace so those who can afford to repay can borrow." The regulator also notes that around 99% of mortgages taken out since 2014 are not in arrears, despite rising interest rates and living costs. The press release does not set out how that figure was calculated.

The six areas of proposals

According to a law-firm summary of the paper, the proposals cover the following.

Interest-only and part-and-part mortgages. Three changes are proposed: adapt the requirements for when a credible repayment strategy is needed, add examples of credible repayment strategy options, and clarify expectations for reviews, with examples of review trigger points. The press release says most borrowers would still need a clear repayment plan unless they are borrowing a smaller amount.

Retirement interest-only mortgages. Current guidance sections would be removed so that joint retirement interest-only applications are assessed in the same way as standard joint mortgages. Firms would not always have to consider whether a sole borrower can afford the loan if a joint borrower dies. The press release presents this as making it easier to unlock property wealth for older borrowers.

Variable and irregular income. The FCA would expand its guidance with examples of the evidence that can be used to assess affordability, and clarify that lenders may agree payment schedules at non-monthly frequencies, such as quarterly. The press release names self-employed people as a group that could benefit.

Foreign-currency loans. The standards for loans denominated in a foreign currency would be separated from those for loans where the borrower's income is in a non-sterling currency. The stated aim is to move from prescriptive rules derived from the Mortgage Credit Directive to an outcomes-focused approach consistent with the Consumer Duty, the FCA's standard for how firms treat retail customers.

Credit-impaired customers. The 'credit-impaired customer' definition would apply only in MCOB 11.6.16R, in the advice example at MCOB 4.7A.22 G, and in SUP 16.12 reporting. Firms could set their own credit risk appetite and target markets, but would be expected not to treat the glossary definition as a factual sign of unaffordability.

Bridging loans. The Handbook definition of regulated bridging loans would be amended to include terms of up to 24 months, and the total term, including the original term and any extensions, would be capped at 24 months. The summary says the FCA states that these proposals do not overlap or conflict with the statutory exemptions in the Financial Services and Markets Act 2000 (Regulated Activities) Order 2001.

Timing

Responses were requested by July 28, 2026. The summary says the FCA intends to publish a policy statement, which would contain the final rules, in the second half of 2026, and gives no more specific date. This article does not cover any policy statement published since, so readers should check the FCA's website for the current position. The press release adds that the FCA is using an online tool to gather consumers' experiences of the mortgage market, alongside feedback from firms.

What the sources do not say

Some points are not in the press release or the summaries cited here. They do not mention changes to loan-to-income limits, and this article therefore does not describe any. They do not give figures for how many more people might obtain a mortgage, and they do not give a date on which changes would take effect. The press release also does not describe advice-specific proposals beyond the reference to the advice example in the Handbook.

How to read the proposals

Three points help. First, a consultation lists what the regulator proposes, and the final text can differ after responses are considered. Second, several of the proposals concern guidance and definitions rather than new limits, so their effect depends on how lenders choose to use the extra flexibility. Third, the bridging loan proposal is about how the regulatory definition is drawn, and it is separate from the affordability themes in the press release.

What to watch

The next milestone is the policy statement. Readers should look for whether the six areas survive unchanged, how the final wording treats the credit-impaired definition, and whether lenders announce changes to their own criteria. This article is a summary of public documents and is not mortgage or legal advice.
source_name: Financial Conduct Authority (press release of June 9, 2026) with CP26/18 summaries from Regulation Tomorrow and CMS
image_alt: UK houses representing mortgage access and affordability (illustrative)
key_points: The FCA published CP26/18, 'Mortgage Rule Review: Supporting first-time buyers and underserved consumers', on June 9, 2026, with responses due by July 28, 2026 and a policy statement intended for the second half of 2026.

It proposes changes in six areas: interest-only and part-and-part mortgages, retirement interest-only, variable and irregular income, foreign-currency loans, the credit-impaired definition and bridging loans.

Lenders would get examples of affordability evidence for variable income and clarity that they may agree payment schedules at non-monthly frequencies, such as quarterly, while the 'credit-impaired customer' definition would apply in only three places in the Handbook.
Regulated bridging loans would be defined to include terms of up to 24 months, with a cap of 24 months on the total term including any extensions.

The FCA says around 99% of mortgages taken out since 2014 are not in arrears, and its executive director David Geale said that mortgage rules need to keep pace so those who can afford to repay can borrow.
why_it_matters: Mortgage rules decide who can borrow and on what terms, so changes aimed at the self-employed, older borrowers and people with a past credit blip could affect real borrowing decisions. The consultation is a proposal rather than a rule change, so nothing changes for borrowers or lenders until the FCA publishes final rules.

title: MAS Names 42 Finalists for the 2026 Global FinTech Hackcelerator and Awards, With Zurich Insurance Challenging Startups to Help SMEs Quantify Business Risk
summary: The Monetary Authority of Singapore announced 42 finalists on October 19, 2026 for the Global FinTech Hackcelerator and SFF FinTech Excellence Awards, including 18 solutions to challenges from GXS Bank, Julius Baer and Zurich Insurance, with demo day on November 18 and winners revealed on November 19.
description:
Singapore's financial regulator has moved its annual fintech competition from the application stage to the finals, and the shortlist shows what banks and insurers want from startups. The Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) announced on October 19, 2026 that 42 finalists had been chosen for the 2026 Global FinTech Hackcelerator and the SFF FinTech Excellence Awards. MAS had invited applications for both programmes in June 2026, with an earlier outline describing a focus on artificial intelligence in banking, wealth management and risk assessment for small businesses. The finalist announcement confirms those themes and sets the dates for the final stage.

The Global FinTech Hackcelerator is organised by MAS together with the Global Finance and Technology Network (GFTN), a not-for-profit entity set up by MAS. It works by asking established companies, called corporate champions, to set a problem and inviting fintech firms around the world to propose market-ready solutions. This year's three champions and challenges are GXS Bank, a digital bank, which asked for integration of credit and fraud risk modelling in digital banking; Julius Baer, a global wealth manager, which asked how to reimagine wealth management for a digitally native generation; and Zurich Insurance, which asked for help enabling small and medium-sized enterprises to better assess, quantify and proactively manage their business risk exposure. Eighteen finalists were shortlisted. The release names the categories but, in the version reviewed, does not list the finalists themselves, which are in annexes to the announcement.

Prizes and follow-on support are specified. There is one winner per problem statement, three in total, and each receives S$80,000. Finalists can explore pilot engagements with their corporate champion, and can apply for the Global FinTech Hackcelerator Scale-Up Grant under the Financial Sector Technology and Innovation scheme, known as FSTI 4.0. The grant provides follow-on funding for product development, commercial milestones and establishing a presence in Singapore. The finalists present their solutions at a Demo Day on November 18, 2026, held as part of the Singapore FinTech Festival (SFF), which runs from November 18 to 20.

The second programme, the SFF FinTech Excellence Awards, is organised by MAS and the Singapore FinTech Association (SFA), supported by PwC Singapore. It recognises corporates and individuals whose initiatives have significantly contributed to the fintech ecosystem and advanced innovation in financial services. The awards received 131 submissions across six categories. In the five corporate categories there were 119 submissions, and four finalists were shortlisted in each, for 20 in total. The categories are Emerging FinTech, Financial Inclusivity, Regulatory Leader, Sustainable Innovator and a thematic award for AI Champion, and each has one winner receiving S$50,000. The individual category, the FinTech Mentor Award, received 13 submissions and four finalists, of whom three will win S$5,000 each. Adding up the 18 Hackcelerator finalists, 20 corporate finalists and four mentor finalists gives the total of 42 in the announcement. Winners will be revealed at the awards dinner on November 19, 2026.

Eleven organisations contributed to the FinTech Gives Back initiative this year, which supports promising fintech innovators: Finmo, Ripple, HeyMax, Aspire, dtcpay, Experian, LexisNexis, Sfye, Sumsub, Width and YouTrip. Kenneth Gay, MAS's chief fintech officer, said the Hackcelerator and Awards aim to help promising fintech solutions gain industry traction and scale into regional and global markets. SFA president Holly Fang noted that 2026 marks the association's tenth year, and Wong Wanyi of PwC Singapore said the awards are entering a new chapter after their tenth anniversary.

The announcement sits within a wider set of MAS initiatives that the release lists. On July 3, 2026, MAS and industry published a white paper called Safeguards for Agentic Finance at Runtime, or SAFR, on safeguards for AI agents in finance, developed under the BuildFin.ai initiative. On August 26, SFF 2026 was announced with a theme of exploring five forces reshaping global finance. And on August 31, MAS committed S$220 million over three years under the renewed FSTI 4.0 scheme. Together they show a regulator that backs both the technology and the rules around it.

For the insurance sector, the Zurich challenge is the most relevant element. Small and medium-sized businesses often struggle to understand what risks they face and how much cover they need, and insurers struggle to assess those risks cheaply. A solution that helps an owner of a small firm quantify exposures could, in principle, lead to better-targeted cover and lower distribution costs, though the announcement does not describe any specific product and no results can be expected until after the demo day. What readers can verify is the structure: a regulator-backed contest, three corporate problems, S$80,000 for each winner and a route to pilots and grants.

What to watch next is the Demo Day on November 18 and the awards dinner on November 19, where the winners will be named. After that, the useful signs will be whether winners secure pilots with their corporate champions and whether any move to set up in Singapore through the scale-up grant. The competition does not guarantee commercial results, but it shows what problems major financial firms are willing to put in front of startups.
source_name: Monetary Authority of Singapore (October 19, 2026) and MAS media release inviting applications (June 2026)

The Hackcelerator challenges come from GXS Bank on integrating credit and fraud risk modelling, Julius Baer on wealth management for a digitally native generation, and Zurich Insurance on helping SMEs assess, quantify and manage business risk.

There is one winner per challenge, each receiving S$80,000, and finalists can seek pilots with the corporate champion and apply for a Global FinTech Hackcelerator Scale-Up Grant under the FSTI 4.0 scheme.
The awards drew 131 submissions, with five corporate categories paying S$50,000 per winner and three Mentor Award winners receiving S$5,000 each.

Demo Day is November 18, 2026, the awards dinner is November 19 and the Singapore FinTech Festival runs November 18 to 20, while MAS committed S$220 million over three years under FSTI 4.0 on August 31.
why_it_matters: Singapore's regulator uses these programmes to steer fintech effort toward problems that banks and insurers say they have. The insurance challenge, helping small businesses measure their risk, shows where regulators and insurers think technology could close the protection gap for smaller firms.

title: Buy Now, Pay Later Became FCA-Regulated on July 15, 2026: Affordability Checks, Ombudsman Access and Section 75 Refund Rights for Interest-Free Instalment Credit
summary: From July 15, 2026, UK interest-free 'Deferred Payment Credit' offered by a lender separate from the retailer is regulated by the FCA under policy statement PS26/1: lenders must check affordability, give key information, and customers can use the Financial Ombudsman and, in some cases, Section 75 refund rights.
description:
Buy Now, Pay Later (BNPL), the interest-free instalment option that appears at online and in-store checkouts, has been brought inside the UK's financial regulation. The Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) calls the product Deferred Payment Credit, or DPC, and the new regime began on July 15, 2026. The FCA published its final rules on February 11, 2026, in policy statement PS26/1, after legislation was published in July 2025. According to analysis by the law firm A&O Shearman, the FCA made only minor amendments to its draft rules and guidance, which were set out in consultation paper CP25/23.

The scale of the market explains the interest. A&O Shearman's summary says the BNPL market grew from £0.06 billion in 2017 to over £13 billion in 2024. For years it sat largely outside consumer credit regulation, partly because interest-free, short-term credit was exempt.

What is covered? The FCA's consumer page explains that the regulated product is interest-free credit repayable in 12 or fewer instalments over 12 months or less. It is regulated when the lender and the supplier of the goods or services are different businesses, as is typical when a shopper uses a third-party BNPL provider at a retailer's checkout. Credit offered by the same business that is selling the goods is not regulated under this regime. Importantly, agreements taken out before July 15, 2026 remain unregulated, so the new protections do not apply retrospectively.

What must lenders do? According to the FCA, lenders must hold FCA authorisation or be registered under the temporary permissions regime to offer DPC. They must check that the customer can afford to repay before the agreement starts. A&O Shearman notes that lenders must assess creditworthiness for each DPC transaction, including those under £50, and that the FCA did not change the existing rules in its consumer credit sourcebook on this point. Lenders must give key information beforehand, including the amount to be borrowed, repayment dates and amounts, the late fee and the customer's rights and protections. If a customer misses a repayment, the lender must make contact and explain what it means, and must support customers who are struggling to repay.

The final rules softened some requirements. A&O Shearman reports that the amount of information in the key product information document was reduced: details on withdrawal, cancellation, early repayment, complaint rights to the Financial Ombudsman Service (FOS) and continuous payment authority move to "additional product information", although the key information must point customers to it. Lenders must tell customers whether they will, or may, check a credit reference agency before deciding on an agreement. Communications about missed payments need to explain the consequences arising from that missed payment, rather than every possible future consequence. Before terminating an agreement or taking enforcement action, firms must signpost free, impartial debt advice. Lenders no longer have to notify guarantors of missed payments. Unauthorised DPC lenders had to comply with the Consumer Duty by July 15, 2026.

One point that differs from the consultation concerns the Financial Ombudsman Service. A&O Shearman reports that the FOS voluntary jurisdiction does not cover DPC, contrary to what the consultation proposed, and that it excludes complaints before regulation began and activity from establishments in the EEA or Gibraltar. For consumers, the FCA's page says that if something goes wrong, they should complain to the lender first and, if unhappy with the response, can escalate to the Financial Ombudsman Service. The FCA also says people may be able to get a refund from the lender under Section 75 of the Consumer Credit Act, the same protection they would have when paying by credit card, subject to the conditions of that law.

The transition arrangements prevent a sudden gap in the market. Firms that were carrying on DPC as of July 15, 2025 without the necessary permissions could register for the temporary permissions regime during a notification window that ran from May 15 to July 1, 2026. Those firms then have six months after July 15, 2026 to apply for full authorisation. The FCA's page tells consumers to check lenders using the FCA Firm Checker, selecting "Borrowing money, including credit card lending and credit information", and says the temporary permissions list includes 15 lenders, such as Clearpay and PayItMonthly. The six-month window means those firms must apply for full authorisation by about mid-January 2027.

Consumers get a few practical benefits. They should see clearer information before they sign up, an affordability assessment that may sometimes lead to a refusal, and contact and support if they fall behind. For those in financial difficulty, the FCA directs people to MoneyHelper's Debt Advice Locator to find free local services.

Two limits are worth remembering. First, the regime covers interest-free credit from a separate lender; other types of credit, such as credit cards or loans, are already regulated through other rules. Second, because earlier agreements are outside the regime, someone who took out BNPL in June may not have the same rights as someone who took it out in August.

For retailers, the change matters indirectly. Some BNPL providers may tighten approvals as they implement affordability checks, which could affect conversion rates at checkout, though the sources reviewed do not quantify any such effect. For the market as a whole, the move from light-touch to full regulation is a significant step, and the FCA's decision to run a temporary regime shows it wants products to remain available while standards rise.
source_name: Financial Conduct Authority (consumer BNPL page) and A&O Shearman (analysis of policy statement PS26/1)
image_alt: Online checkout representing Buy Now Pay Later credit (illustrative)
key_points: UK Buy Now, Pay Later, which the FCA calls Deferred Payment Credit (DPC), became regulated on July 15, 2026 under final rules published as PS26/1 on February 11, 2026.

Regulated DPC is interest-free, repayable in 12 or fewer instalments over 12 months or less, and offered by a lender that is a different business from the supplier of the goods; agreements taken out before July 15 stay unregulated.

Lenders must be FCA-authorised or in the temporary permissions regime, check that borrowers can afford repayments (including on transactions under £50), give key product information, contact customers who miss payments and support those in difficulty.
Customers can complain to the lender and then the Financial Ombudsman Service, and may be able to claim a refund from the lender under Section 75 of the Consumer Credit Act.

The FCA lists 15 firms in the temporary permissions regime, including Clearpay and PayItMonthly, and those firms have six months after July 15 to apply for full authorisation; the market grew from £0.06 billion in 2017 to over £13 billion in 2024.
why_it_matters: Millions of UK shoppers use buy now, pay later at checkout, often without thinking of it as borrowing. Regulation means these lenders now face affordability checks and customer-protection rules, and users gain routes for complaints and refunds, though agreements made before July 15 are not covered.

title: KFF's Tracker Counts 11 Insurers Leaving the ACA Marketplaces for 2027 and Seven Entering, as Cigna Exits All 11 States Where It Sells Individual Plans After Enrollment Fell by More Than a Million
summary: KFF's insurer participation tracker, first published on June 11 and updated on October 28, 2026, counts 11 carriers leaving ACA Marketplaces for 2027, fully or in some states, and seven entering new state Marketplaces, with Cigna leaving the individual market in all 11 states where it participates after enrollment fell by more than a million.
description:
More health insurers have announced that they will leave the Affordable Care Act (ACA) Marketplaces for 2027 than have announced they will enter them. That is the picture in the insurer participation tracker maintained by KFF, the health policy research organisation. KFF first published the brief on June 11, 2026 and updated it on October 28, 2026. KFF warns that the information may change as insurers make further announcements, and this article reports the tracker as it stood at the October update. The portion of the page reviewed for this article does not name most of the carriers, so it describes the totals and the one insurer the text names, Cigna.

The totals

As of October 28, KFF counts 11 carriers that have announced they will leave ACA Marketplaces for plan year 2027, either completely or in some of the states where they operate. Seven carriers have announced they will enter new state Marketplaces. The exits therefore outnumber the entries by four, calculated here, although the tracker counts carriers, not enrollees, so the numbers do not show how many people are affected on either side.

KFF groups insurers by parent company and compiled the data from several sources: Mark Farrah Associates enrollment data, the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) Qualified Health Plan landscape files, CMS medical loss ratio public use files, HIX Compare data from the Robert Wood Johnson Foundation, Healthinsurance.org and press materials.

Cigna

The one carrier the reviewed text describes in detail is Cigna. It is leaving the individual market in 2027 to focus on other segments, citing limited potential to grow its ACA business. Cigna reported more than 350,000 on-exchange enrollees in the first quarter of 2026 and will exit all 11 states in which it participates, both on and off the exchange. This article does not report an enrollment figure beyond the 350,000, because the text reviewed gives no other number. Members of a departing insurer generally have to pick a new plan during open enrollment, but the tracker does not discuss the mechanics, and consumers should rely on notices from their insurer and their state Marketplace.

Why insurers are pulling back

KFF links the changes to the expiration of the enhanced premium tax credits at the end of 2025. Enrollment fell by more than a million between the 2025 and 2026 open enrollment periods, and KFF expects further declines during 2026. KFF adds that enrollment declines could shrink the risk pool if healthier enrollees drop coverage, which would leave a sicker pool on average.

The same concern appears in KFF's separate analysis of proposed 2027 premiums, reported in July by MedCity News and the Associated Press. That analysis found a median proposed increase of 14% across 77 insurers in 16 states and Washington, D.C., and said insurers expected the market to keep deteriorating in 2027. Those proposals were preliminary, and this article has not verified the final approved rates.

What fewer insurers could mean

KFF notes that some states have more than one insurer exiting. In those states, consumers may have fewer choices and competition may decline. The tracker does not say in which states, and the text reviewed does not list them. It would be wrong to assume that every state faces a loss of choice, because seven carriers are entering new state Marketplaces, and some of those entries could offset exits in particular states. The tracker as reviewed does not say.

What the tracker does not say

The reviewed text does not name the other 10 exiting carriers, does not name the entrants, does not give the total number of affected enrollees and does not list the affected states. KFF's page evidently contains a table with that detail, which was not part of the text available. This article therefore does not make claims about any carrier other than Cigna. It also does not say how many counties will be left with a single insurer, because the tracker as reviewed gives no such figure.

The tracker is explicitly a running record. KFF says insurer information may change, which means that both the 11 exits and the seven entries could be revised by the time open enrollment starts. Readers should check the current version of the tracker and their state Marketplace for the carriers available where they live.

How the tracker was built

Because the tracker groups insurers by parent company, a single parent that sells under several brand names counts once. That affects comparisons: a count of carriers is not a count of plans, and one parent exiting a state can remove several plans at once. The tracker is also built from enrollment data, regulatory filings and press materials.

What consumers can do

The tracker is a research brief, not consumer guidance, but its findings point to some practical steps. People covered by an insurer that is leaving should watch for a notice from the insurer and their state Marketplace and compare the plans available in their area, including premiums, deductibles and provider networks. Anyone with a subsidy should check how it applies to a new plan. Those who stay with an insurer that is not leaving should still review their renewal notice, because premiums and benefits can change from year to year.
source_name: KFF (Tracking Insurer Participation Changes in the ACA Marketplaces in 2027, updated October 28, 2026)
image_alt: Medical files and insurance forms representing health coverage changes (illustrative)
key_points: KFF's tracker, first published on June 11, 2026 and updated on October 28, 2026, counts 11 carriers announcing they will leave ACA Marketplaces for plan year 2027, fully or in some states, and seven announcing entry into new state Marketplaces.

Cigna is leaving the individual market in 2027 to focus on other segments, citing limited potential to grow its ACA business; it reported more than 350,000 first-quarter on-exchange enrollees and will exit all 11 states where it participates, on and off the exchange.

Enrollment fell by more than a million between the 2025 and 2026 open enrollment periods after the enhanced premium tax credits expired at the end of 2025, and KFF expects further declines during 2026.
Some states have more than one insurer exiting, which may leave consumers with fewer choices and less competition, and falling enrollment could shrink the risk pool if healthier people drop coverage.
KFF says insurer information may change, and the text reviewed does not name the other exiting or entering carriers or give a total number of affected enrollees.
why_it_matters: When an insurer leaves a state's individual market, its members must choose a new plan, and in places with few carriers the remaining choices matter for price and networks. The tracker shows how the end of the enhanced subsidies is feeding into insurers' decisions about where to sell.
